analysis.one_liner: Opens federal land and waters to oil, gas and coal development and strips EPA climate rules.
analysis.headline: Referred to six House committees and never received a vote; it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the ban on exporting crude oil, opened the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and other federal lands and offshore areas to drilling, handed states the option to take over energy development on federal land, and rewritten environmental law to remove climate rules, weaken the Endangered Species Act, and speed up drilling permits. It was pitched as a jobs and growth measure but its main beneficiaries would have been oil, gas, and coal companies.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil, gas, and coal companies would gain new export markets, mandatory lease sales, drilling permits that are automatically approved if the government misses a 60-day deadline, and sharply reduced ability of the public or courts to challenge leases. TransCanada would get its Keystone XL pipeline approved without a presidential permit. States that opted in could run energy development on federal land under their own rules with no federal judicial review. Some provisions would also benefit tribes, including letting the Navajo Nation approve long-term leases without the Interior Department's sign-off.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals presidential authority to restrict exports of oil, petroleum products, coal, and natural gas, and directs Commerce to grant crude oil export licenses except to sanctioned countries

Repeals the prohibition on oil and gas leasing in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and orders competitive leasing on the Coastal Plain, with a 1987 environmental study deemed to satisfy all National Environmental Policy Act requirements

Requires an offshore lease sale every 270 days in any planning area with commercial interest, deems drilling permits approved if not decided within 60 days, and charges a $5,000 fee for each administrative protest, with unsettled protests automatically denied

Lets a state elect to take over energy development on federal land in that state, with the state's program deemed to satisfy federal environmental law and its activities exempt from federal judicial review and the Administrative Procedure Act

Redefines 'air pollutant' under the Clean Air Act to exclude greenhouse gases, voids pending EPA carbon rules, and declares that five major environmental laws neither authorize nor require climate regulation
Grants states sole authority over hydraulic fracturing, including on federal land, and declares federal fracking rules inapplicable on Indian trust land without tribal consent
Approves the Keystone XL pipeline without a presidential permit, deems its 2014 environmental review complete, and channels any court challenge solely to the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals
Includes tribal provisions letting the Navajo Nation enter 99-year and mineral leases under approved tribal regulations without Interior Department approval

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the environmental and climate costs: the bill removes the main federal tools for limiting carbon emissions, forbids weighing the overseas effects of exported coal, opens the Arctic refuge to drilling, and cuts back citizens' ability to contest leases through protests, attorney fee awards, or lawsuits. Taxpayers would also forgo a stronger federal hand in managing public lands and royalties.

drawbacks.text: The bill deems oil and gas leasing in the Arctic refuge compatible with the refuge's purposes without any new findings, and forbids the Interior Secretary from even analyzing a no-leasing alternative in environmental reviews
Stripping greenhouse gases from the Clean Air Act and voiding EPA carbon rules would remove the principal federal mechanism for addressing climate change

Deemed-approved drilling permits, a $5,000 fee per protest, automatic denial of unresolved protests, bans on attorney fee awards, and 60-day limits on injunctions would sharply reduce the public's ability to challenge energy projects on federal land
Supporters would acknowledge that the state-takeover option, with no federal judicial review and no Administrative Procedure Act coverage, removes standard checks on how public lands are developed

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated aim — faster permitting, more domestic energy, and export access — had some real-world support: the crude oil export ban was widely seen as a relic of the 1970s. But the bill bundled that idea with sweeping environmental rollbacks: gutting climate regulation, weakening the Endangered Species Act to a pay-to-play cost-benefit test, opening the Arctic refuge with pre-ordained environmental findings, and making it expensive and procedurally difficult for citizens to object. For everyday people, the climate and air-quality costs and the loss of recourse would very likely have outweighed any consumer benefit, and the design gave away public land decisions to whichever state opted in.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to six House committees and various subcommittees, none of which ever acted on it, and it died quietly when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Bridenstine introduced the American Energy Renaissance Act of 2015 in the House on March 19, 2015, joined by Reps. DesJarlais, Duncan of South Carolina, and Jordan as original cosponsors
The bill was referred the same day to six committees: Natural Resources, Transportation and Infrastructure, Energy and Commerce, Agriculture, the Judiciary, and Foreign Affairs

Over the following three weeks it was referred to subcommittees on energy and power, water resources, railroads and pipelines, coast guard and maritime, conservation and forestry, energy and mineral resources, and Indian and Alaska Native affairs
No committee ever reported the bill, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2017 with the bill still stalled in committee

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, existing environmental protections, federal management of public lands, and citizens' ability to challenge energy projects remained in place. Oil, gas, and coal companies did not get the expanded access and export and permitting provisions this bill would have given them, though separate legislation in the same Congress later enacted parts of the export agenda.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public lands and environmental rules stayed intact

for.name: Jim Bridenstine
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee (and five other committees)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no committee ever reported it for a floor vote

against.name: Speaker of the House
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor in two Congress sessions

against.name: President Obama
against.what_they_did: Opposed congressional efforts to force Keystone XL approval and expand fossil fuel development on federal land, and would have vetoed such measures

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support; the bill died in committee without any vote being taken.

industries.note: The bill repeals oil export limits, mandates offshore lease sales every 270 days, deems drilling permits approved after 60 days, opens the Arctic refuge and the National Petroleum Reserve to leasing, and lets states take over federal-land energy development with no judicial review. Its industry gains come directly at the expense of environmental protections the public otherwise holds.

Repeals presidential authority to restrict coal exports and directs that environmental reviews of coal terminals consider only domestic impacts, ignoring pollution from burning the coal overseas. The public bears the downstream climate effect the bill forbids agencies to weigh.

Keystone XL would be approved without a presidential permit, its environmental review deemed complete, and challenges funneled to a single friendly court. This short-circuits the permitting review process for a project affecting land and water across the country.
Repealing the renewable fuel standard removes blending mandates refiners oppose, but lifting the crude export ban would end refiners' access to discounted domestic crude, raising their input costs.

industries.industry: Corn ethanol and renewable fuel producers
industries.note: The bill phases out the renewable fuel standard, eliminating the mandated market for ethanol and biodiesel. That helps refiners and motorists at the margin but removes a major support for the farm-belt biofuel industry.

The bill bars attorney fee awards in cases that reduce resource production or jobs, imposes a $5,000 protest fee, restricts standing, and caps injunctions at 60 days, sharply limiting the public-interest groups and citizens who challenge federal energy decisions.
